Vignette:
# Aroha's Reckoning

Aroha had always prided herself on control. At sixty-three, she had spent four decades climbing the corporate ladder, managing timelines and budgets with the precision of someone who understood that attention to detail kept chaos at bay. Her Samoan mother had raised her to be self-reliant, and Aroha had internalized that lesson so thoroughly that asking for help felt like a betrayal of something fundamental in herself. But in the autumn of 2022, control had been taken from her in a way that no spreadsheet or delegation could reverse.

The diagnosis came during what should have been a routine colonoscopy. The gastroenterologist's face had changed mid-procedure—that infinitesimal shift in expression that Aroha's body registered before her conscious mind caught up. Colon cancer, stage three. What followed was a blur of consultations, scans, and a surgical oncology team explaining lymph node involvement and adjuvant chemotherapy regimens. Aroha remembered the surgeon's hands gesturing over her abdomen as if it were a map of contested territory. She remembered the anesthesiologist explaining sedation before her first infusion, and then the needle—a thick-gauge IV line going into her forearm—and the sensation of her body becoming something foreign, something being invaded and colonized by medical machinery and poison meant to save her.

The chemotherapy lasted six months. Aroha had endured it with the same grim determination she brought to everything, arriving at her oncology appointments on schedule, sitting in the reclining chair while nurses accessed her port, watching the clear fluid drip down the tubing into her chest. But something in her had fractured during those months in ways that surgery and chemotherapy could not touch. She had lost her hair. Her body had become skeletal, then bloated with fluid retention. She had spent nights vomiting, days unable to leave the bathroom, weeks when her hands were so numb from neuropathy that she could barely hold a pen. The woman in the mirror was unrecognizable, and Aroha had come to associate that stranger with a body that had betrayed her, that could no longer be trusted to simply exist without threatening her life.

Now, nearly two years into remission, Aroha found herself unable to move past what had happened. Her oncologist had cleared her. The scans were clean. But her mind and body had not received that message. When her husband, David, tried to touch her shoulder unexpectedly, she would flinch violently, her nervous system perceiving threat in his hand. Conversations with friends about their own health concerns—a friend's mammogram, a colleague's arthritis—would trigger a flooding sense that her life was over, that the cancer was still eating through her, that she was living on borrowed time in a body that could betray her at any moment. She had come to believe that the cancer had destroyed everything: her sense of safety, her sense of self, her capacity to trust the basic machinery of her own flesh.

At work, the impact had become undeniable. Aroha had always been the project manager who could hold a dozen threads simultaneously, who never missed a deadline. But in recent months, she had found herself unable to concentrate during meetings. Her mind would drift, or worse, snap suddenly into vivid recall—not just memory but a complete sensory flooding. She would be sitting in a conference room and suddenly feel herself back in the oncology chair, smell the clinical smell of the infusion center, feel the needle sliding into her port, taste the metallic tang of the medication. Her body would lock into the same posture she had held during those treatments, shoulders hunched, jaw clenched. Her colleagues had begun to notice. Her manager had gently suggested that perhaps she was overextended. Aroha had not told him that she was having panic attacks in the bathroom before client presentations, or that she had turned down a promotion because the increased visibility and pressure felt impossible to manage.

The particular cruelty was that Aroha could not even articulate what had happened to her in a way that made sense. When David asked her to explain why she was so angry, why she had snapped at him over something trivial, she found herself unable to put words to the terror that lived in her now. It was not something she could think through logically. It was something her body knew—a wordless knowing that she was unsafe, that her own cells could turn against her, that the medical system that had supposedly saved her had also marked her as someone whose body was fundamentally unreliable.

It was David who finally insisted she see someone. He had watched his wife disappear into a fog of irritability and fear, and he had reached the limit of his patience and his helplessness. Aroha had resisted, convinced that talking about it would only make it more real. But sitting in the waiting room of the trauma-informed therapist's office, she was beginning to wonder if perhaps the weight of carrying this alone had already made it as real as it could possibly be.
